question: What is the Big-O running time of a linear search over a list of n items?
correct: O(n)
incorrect: O(log n)
O(n²)
feedback: In the worst case a linear search checks every item, so the work grows in proportion to n: O(n).

question: NPC: Halving the shelf
intro: The library runs deeper than the torchlight reaches. Ada rests a hand on a shelf of numbered ledgers. “Fifteen ledgers, already in order. A slow apprentice starts at the left. Watch what a fast one does.”

steps.say: I want ledger 23. I don't touch the first ledger — I go straight to the MIDDLE one. It reads 20. Since 23 is bigger than 20, and the shelf is sorted, every ledger from the middle leftwards is out. Eight ledgers eliminated by looking at one.
Seven remain, to the right of where I looked.

check.answer: The middle of the seven that remain
wrong: The first of the seven that remain
The last ledger on the whole shelf
check.why: Every pass repeats the same move on whatever is left — that is what makes it halve so fast.

steps.say: The counts go 15, then 7, then 3, then 1. Four looks at worst. Double the shelf to 31 and it costs just ONE more look — that is what O(log n) means. All of it depends on the shelf being sorted; on an unsorted shelf this trick is worthless.

outro: “Now put the moves in order yourself.”

question: Arrange the moves of one pass of binary search over a sorted list.
items: Look at the item in the middle of the range still in play
Compare that item with the target
Discard the half that cannot contain the target
Repeat on the half that remains
feedback: Each pass looks at the middle, compares, throws away the half the target cannot be in, and repeats on the rest — which is why the work grows only logarithmically.

question: What does binary search do on each pass?
correct: Compares the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain it
incorrect: Compares the first two items and swaps them if they are out of order
Removes the middle item and searches the rest from the start
Splits the list into single items and merges them back in order
feedback: This is how you look a word up in a dictionary: open to the middle, decide whether the word is earlier or later, and ignore the half it cannot be in. Each look halves what remains.

question: In our search functions, what value signals 'not found'?
correct: None, Python's built-in 'nothing here' value
incorrect: -1, the way many other languages do it
0, since it is the first list index
An empty list with no items in it
feedback: We return None as the sentinel for 'not found'. Avoid -1 in Python, because -1 is a valid index meaning the last item.

question: A search that repeatedly halves a sorted list to find a target is called a ___ search.
correct: binary
feedback: Binary search halves the remaining items each step, giving O(log n) running time on sorted data.

question: Which Big-O describes linear search, and which describes binary search?
correct: Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n)
incorrect: Linear search is O(log n); binary search is O(n)
Both are O(n), but binary search has a smaller constant
Linear search is O(1); binary search is O(n log n)
feedback: Doubling the list doubles linear search's worst case, but adds only one step to binary search. Among a billion items, linear search may check a billion and binary search checks about 30.

question: Order these growth rates from fastest-growing to slowest-growing for large n. Which grows the fastest?
correct: O(n²)
incorrect: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
feedback: For large n, O(n²) grows fastest, then O(n log n), then O(n), then O(log n). Slower growth means a more scalable algorithm.

question: Which Big-O describes work that stays the same no matter how big the input is?
incorrect: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
feedback: O(1) is constant time: the work does not change as n grows, like reading one item by its index.

question: Match each Big-O class to a description of how its work grows.

pairs.definition: Constant: the same work for any input size
Grows slowly, like repeatedly halving the data
Grows in direct proportion to the input
Grows with the square of the input

feedback: These classes rank how fast work grows: constant, logarithmic, linear, and quadratic, from most to least scalable.

question: Arrange these growth rates from slowest-growing to fastest-growing as n gets large.
feedback: Constant work never grows; logarithmic barely does; linear keeps pace with the input; n log n is a little worse, which is why merge sort beats selection sort; and quadratic climbs sharply, doubling the input roughly quadrupling the work.

question: How does selection sort work?
correct: Find the smallest remaining item, swap it into place, and repeat
incorrect: Split the list in half repeatedly, then merge the sorted halves
Compare neighboring pairs and swap them until no swaps remain
Insert each item into a second list at the right position
feedback: The outer loop walks the slot being filled and the inner loop scans the unsorted tail for the smallest item. After each pass, the sorted front of the list grows by one.

question: Match each algorithm to its typical Big-O running time.
feedback: Knowing an algorithm's Big-O lets you predict how it will scale before you ever run it on large data.

question: NPC: One pass of selection sort
intro: Ada lays five numbered tiles face-up: 5, 3, 9, 1, 6. “Selection sort is the one people mis-describe. It does not shuffle things along. It picks, and it swaps. One pass.”

steps.say: The sorted part grows from the front. Pass one, so position 0 is the slot I am filling. To fill it I scan the WHOLE row for the smallest tile. Scanning 5, 3, 9, 1, 6 — the smallest is 1, sitting in position 3.
Now the move that people get wrong.

check.prompt: The smallest tile is 1, at position 3. How does it reach position 0?
check.answer: It swaps places with the tile currently in position 0
wrong: Everything between them shifts right to make room
It is removed and appended to the end
check.why: Selection sort swaps just those two tiles. Nothing else moves — that is what makes one pass cheap.

steps.say: So 1 and 5 trade places and the row reads 1, 3, 9, 5, 6. Note that 5 landed where 1 used to be, and 3, 9, 6 never moved. Position 0 is finished forever; pass two scans only what is left.

outro: “Same move, different tiles, next question. Scan for the smallest, then swap it to the front.”

question: Given  ranks = [7, 2, 10, 4, 1], what does the list look like after the FIRST pass of selection sort?
feedback: The first pass finds the smallest item (1, at the end) and swaps it with whatever was in slot 0. The 7 that was displaced moves to where the 1 had been.

question: Why is selection sort O(n squared)?
correct: For each of the n slots it scans the rest, so work multiplies
incorrect: It has to sort the list twice to be certain it is in order
Each swap requires copying the whole list into a new one
It compares every item to every other item exactly twice
feedback: A scan inside a loop means roughly n times n comparisons. Fine for a handful of cards; for a million items that is about a trillion comparisons.

question: What is the Big-O running time of selection sort?
correct: O(n²)
incorrect: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
feedback: Selection sort scans the remaining items on every pass, so its work grows with the square of n: O(n²).

question: Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Which description matches it?
correct: Split until each pile is one item, then merge sorted piles upward
incorrect: Scan for the smallest item, place it, and repeat on the rest
Sort the first half completely, then append the second half unsorted
Compare the first and last items and work inwards to the middle
feedback: A single item is already sorted, and merging two sorted piles is cheap. There are about log n levels of splitting, each doing O(n) merging work, which is where O(n log n) comes from.

question: Why is merge sort (O(n log n)) usually preferred over selection sort (O(n²)) for large lists?
correct: Its work grows much more slowly as the list gets large
incorrect: It does not need to compare any of the items
It only works on lists that are already sorted
It uses no extra memory of any kind at all
feedback: For large n, O(n log n) grows far slower than O(n²), so merge sort scales to big inputs that would make selection sort painfully slow.

question: Which of these are true about  sorted(items)  and  items.sort()? (Select all that apply)
correct: sorted(items) returns a new list and leaves the original alone
items.sort() rearranges the original list and returns None
incorrect: Both leave the original list unchanged
sorted(items) only works on lists of numbers
items.sort() must be given a key function to work
feedback: Writing x = mylist.sort() and getting None back is a classic beginner bug. Use sorted() when you want a new list, and .sort() when you mean to rearrange the original in place.

question: You need to search a large collection many times, and you are free to prepare it first. Which approach is best?
correct: Sort it once, then use binary search for every lookup
incorrect: Use linear search each time and skip the sorting cost
Sort it again before every single lookup
Use selection sort during each lookup to find the item
feedback: Sorting is a one-time cost that makes every later search logarithmic. When you search a lot, that trade pays for itself quickly; for a single lookup on unsorted data, plain linear search is simpler.

question: What does the  key  function do in  sorted(words, key=len)?
correct: It sorts by each item's length instead of its value
incorrect: It removes any items whose length is much too long
It reverses the final ordering of the sorted list
It limits the result to just the first len items
feedback: A key function returns the value to sort by. key=len sorts the words by length rather than alphabetically.

question: A special return value meaning "not found", such as the None these search functions return, is called a ___ value.
correct: sentinel
feedback: A sentinel is a value chosen to signal a condition rather than to be real data. Choosing a safe one matters: -1 is a poor sentinel in Python because it is also a valid index.

question: Given a list named nums, write the statement that sorts it in place (modifying nums itself).
correct: nums.sort()
feedback: nums.sort() rearranges nums in place and returns None.

question: Write the one-line Python statement that swaps the values of two variables a and b.
correct: a, b = b, a
b, a = a, b
feedback: a, b = b, a swaps the two values in a single statement using tuple unpacking.

question: Rearranging a list without making a new copy is described as sorting ___ (two words joined by a hyphen).
correct: in-place
in place
feedback: An in-place sort like nums.sort() rearranges the existing list rather than building a new one.

question: What does it mean for a problem to be computable?
correct: There is some algorithm that can solve it
incorrect: It can be solved instantly with no work at all
It can be checked but never actually solved
It can be solved only by a quantum computer
feedback: A problem is computable if some algorithm exists that solves it. Computability is about whether a method exists, not how fast it is.

question: What does the Church-Turing thesis claim?
correct: Anything computable at all can be computed by a Turing machine
incorrect: Any program that halts can be made to run in reasonable time
Every problem has an algorithm if you look hard enough
Turing machines are faster than the computers we build today
feedback: This is why we can speak of computation as one universal idea rather than a different idea per machine. Your phone can compute no class of things that the tape-and-rulebook gadget could not.

question: What does it mean to say the halting problem is undecidable?
correct: No algorithm can answer correctly in every case, whatever its resources
incorrect: The problem takes so long to solve that nobody has finished yet
The answer depends on which programming language is used
The problem can be solved but only by a quantum computer
feedback: Undecidable is not the same as hard. A hard problem can be solved slowly; an undecidable one has no correct general algorithm at all — faster hardware changes nothing.

question: A problem that no algorithm can solve in every case, like the halting problem, is called ___.
correct: undecidable
feedback: Undecidable problems are beyond any algorithm in principle, not just slow or unsolved.

question: Real tools such as antivirus scanners and infinite-loop detectors exist even though the underlying questions are undecidable. How is that possible?
correct: They settle for being usually right, or right on limited cases
incorrect: They run the program to completion first and then report
They rely on hardware that is not a Turing machine
They only work on programs written without any loops
feedback: Undecidability rules out a perfect general answer, not a useful partial one. Practical tools trade completeness for usefulness — which is why an antivirus can miss things and a type checker rejects some safe programs.

question: In complexity theory, what is the class P?
correct: Problems that can be solved quickly by an algorithm
incorrect: Problems whose answers can be checked quickly
Problems that no algorithm can ever solve
Problems that require a Turing machine to state
feedback: P is the class of problems an algorithm can solve quickly (in polynomial time). It is about solving, not just checking.

question: Which pair of statements correctly describes the classes P and NP?
correct: P problems are solved quickly; NP answers can be checked quickly
incorrect: P problems are possible; NP problems are impossible for any computer
P problems need sorted input; NP problems work on unsorted input
P problems run on one processor; NP problems need many processors
feedback: Assembling a thousand-piece jigsaw may be brutal, but glancing at a finished one to confirm it is right is quick. That gap between finding and checking is what P versus NP is about.

question: Why is the question "does P equal NP?" famous?
correct: Nobody has proved it either way, and a proof wins a million dollars
incorrect: It was proved false in 1936 and is now only of historical interest
It asks whether any computer can outperform a Turing machine
It determines how fast a sorting algorithm is allowed to be
feedback: Almost everyone believes finding is genuinely harder than checking, but belief is not proof. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, and much of modern encryption quietly depends on the answer being no.

question: The P vs. NP question is often summarized as which cultural idea?
correct: Is every problem that is easy to check also easy to solve?
incorrect: Is every problem eventually solvable given enough time?
Are computers faster than the people who program them?
Can a Turing machine compute anything a person can?
feedback: P vs. NP asks whether 'easy to check' (NP) implies 'easy to solve' (P). It is a famous open question with no proven answer.

question: What does it mean to call a problem intractable?
correct: It is solvable in principle but needs impractical work
incorrect: It cannot ever be solved by any algorithm at all
It can be solved instantly on almost any computer
It has never been written down at all clearly enough
feedback: Intractable problems have algorithms, but those algorithms need so much time on large inputs that they are useless in practice. This differs from undecidable, which means no algorithm exists.

question: Which of the following statements about the limits of computation are correct? (Select all that apply)
correct: The halting problem cannot be solved by any program, including AI
Some problems are solvable in principle but intractable in practice
Being easy to check does not guarantee a problem is easy to solve
incorrect: A fast enough computer could eventually solve the halting problem
Every problem in NP is already known to be in P
feedback: Undecidable problems like halting are impossible for any program, intractable problems are merely impractical, and whether NP equals P is unknown. No amount of speed crosses the undecidable wall.

question: Which of these are limits about cost rather than about impossibility? (Select all that apply)
correct: Finding the provably best packing for a truck full of oddly shaped boxes
Scheduling five hundred classes with no conflicts, guaranteed optimally
incorrect: Writing one program that decides whether any given program halts
Writing one checker that decides whether any two programs always agree
feedback: The first two are NP-style problems: solutions exist and can be checked quickly, but finding a guaranteed-best one may take impractically long. The last two are undecidable — no correct general algorithm exists at all.

question: Why can't a more powerful AI or LLM solve an undecidable problem like the halting problem?
correct: The limit is mathematical, so no program can cross it
incorrect: AI simply has not been trained on enough examples yet
AI runs on hardware that is currently too slow
AI can solve it, but only one case at a time
feedback: Undecidability is a proven mathematical limit on algorithms themselves. An AI is still a program, so it is bound by the same wall, no matter how capable it becomes.

question: A problem that can be solved in principle, but needs an impractical amount of work to solve, is called ___.
correct: intractable
feedback: Intractable sits between easy and impossible: the algorithm exists, but running it on a real input would take longer than anyone can wait.

question: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a linear search make on a list of {{n}} items?
feedback_template: A linear search may have to check every item, so the worst case on {{n}} items is {{expected}} comparisons.

question: Match each technique to when you would reach for it.

pairs.definition: The data is unsorted or the list is tiny
The data is sorted and you search it often
Learning how sorting works, or a very small list
Real code, where a fast built-in sort is wanted

feedback: In practice you almost never hand-write a sort. Knowing how they work is what lets you judge which tool fits and what it will cost.

question: A sorted list has {{n}} items. At most how many comparisons does a binary search make? (This is floor(log2 n) + 1.)
feedback_template: Binary search halves the list each step, so at most floor(log2 {{n}}) + 1 = {{expected}} comparisons are needed.

question: Write the Python expression that returns a new list holding the items of  nums  in ascending order, without changing nums.
correct: sorted(nums)
feedback: sorted(nums) hands back a new sorted list. nums.sort() would rearrange the original instead and return None.
